segments.flavor: the station ID, landing like the station's signature
segments.text: Daniel: You are with The Brief. Calm news, no noise, and more music in a moment.

segments.flavor: the station ID, landing like the station's signature
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief runs on two simple ideas. Say the thing plainly.
Daniel: Then stop talking and let the piano finish its sentence.

segments.flavor: the station ID, landing like the station's signature
segments.text:
Emma: The Brief, where the headlines are short and the saxophone solos are not.
Emma: Stay exactly where you are. Here comes another one.

segments.flavor: the station ID, landing like the station's signature
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief. Calm news for people with somewhere to be.
Emma: And for the people going nowhere at all. No judgement here.
Daniel: Back to the quiet stuff.

segments.flavor: a calm time check and a one-line tease of what the rest of the hour holds
segments.text:
Daniel: It is a quarter past the hour, and nothing has gone wrong so far.
Daniel: Ahead of us: one short word, one small correction. But first, the long song.

segments.flavor: back-announce the music stream in one warm sentence, then a dry observation from Emma
segments.text:
Daniel: That was a piano trio taking its time, and taking ours along with it.
Emma: Nobody in that band was in a hurry. Nobody in that band has a boss.
Daniel: More of the same, gladly.

segments.flavor: a short 'and finally' style light story, invented but plausible, clearly framed as the hosts' own anecdote
segments.text:
Emma: And finally: my neighbour returned a ladder I lent him two summers ago.
Daniel: That is a happy ending.
Emma: He had painted it a different colour. Anyway, the music.

segments.flavor: a measured public-service style reminder with one dry twist
segments.text:
Daniel: A reminder from the desk. Drink a glass of water before the next coffee.
Daniel: The body is mostly water. Coffee knows that, and the music will wait.

segments.flavor: a calm time check and a one-line tease of what the rest of the hour holds
segments.text:
Daniel: It is half past the hour here on The Brief, and the desk is calm about that.
Daniel: Coming up in this half hour: a forecast, a small apology, and a great deal of saxophone.

segments.flavor: back-announce the music stream in one warm sentence, then a dry observation from Emma
segments.text:
Daniel: That last set came to us from a saxophone in no particular hurry at all.
Emma: It sounded like an apology that went on slightly too long, and I loved it.
Daniel: We will let the horn player explain himself after this next one.

segments.flavor: a short 'and finally' style light story, invented but plausible, clearly framed as the hosts' own anecdote
segments.text:
Daniel: And finally: I found a library book in a coat I had not worn since spring.
Emma: How late is it, exactly?
Daniel: The card inside says it was due at an address I left years ago.
Emma: Return it anyway, quietly, and let this next song cover the sound.

segments.flavor: a measured public-service style reminder with one dry twist
segments.text:
Daniel: A measured reminder from the desk: the smoke alarm in the hallway runs on a battery.
Daniel: That battery waits until the exact middle of the night to mention it. Now, some piano.

segments.flavor: a calm time check and a one-line tease of what the rest of the hour holds
segments.text:
Daniel: Ten minutes to the top of the hour, and The Brief is where you left it.
Emma: Which is here. Still here. Suspiciously here.
Daniel: In these ten minutes: the word of the hour, and one useful fact about rain.
Emma: Before all of that, three more minutes of a man playing a double bass.
Daniel: Take it away, sir.

segments.flavor: back-announce the music stream in one warm sentence, then a dry observation from Emma
segments.text:
Daniel: That was a long, slow piece of music, and it outlasted my tea entirely.
Emma: Your tea had a considerable head start and still lost.
Daniel: The music we lean on here is mostly brushes, rarely sticks, and never shouting.
Emma: A drummer holding a brush is a drummer who has made peace with something.
Daniel: More of that peace, right now.

segments.flavor: a short 'and finally' style light story, invented but plausible, clearly framed as the hosts' own anecdote
segments.text:
Emma: And finally, from my own household: my grandmother labelled every key in the drawer.
Daniel: Sensible.
Emma: Every single label said the same two words. Not this one.
Daniel: So the drawer was a complete map of everything it could not open.
Emma: She called that honest work, and she was never once locked out.
Daniel: Honest work, and a good place to start the music.

segments.flavor: a measured public-service style reminder with one dry twist
segments.text:
Daniel: A public service note from the desk, and this one is genuinely useful.
Emma: Those are my favourite kind. Rare, but my favourite.
Daniel: Write the name on the box before you tape the box shut.
Emma: Otherwise the box becomes a small mystery you have to open twice.
Daniel: A mystery with your own winter coat inside it. Now, the music.

segments.flavor: a calm time check and a one-line tease of what the rest of the hour holds
segments.text:
Daniel: It is coming up on the top of the hour here at The Brief.
Emma: And Sky is somewhere outside the building, which she insists counts as a location.
Sky: [breathless] It counts. It has weather, a bench, and a man feeding three birds.
Daniel: Ahead in the next hour: a forecast, the word of the hour, and Sky recovering.
Sky: The recovery takes longer than the reporting. That is simply the job.
Emma: Take as long as you need. We have a piano to get through first.

segments.flavor: back-announce the music stream in one warm sentence, then a dry observation from Emma
segments.text:
Daniel: That was a quartet who clearly rehearsed in a room with a low ceiling.
Emma: You can hear the ceiling. That is not a criticism.
Daniel: The music on this station is chosen for one quality above all the others.
Emma: Volume?
Daniel: Restraint. Nobody here has ever played a long solo to prove a point.
Emma: One trumpet nearly did. We faded him out with great affection.
Daniel: Stay for this next one. It is four minutes of a man being careful.

segments.flavor: a short 'and finally' style light story, invented but plausible, clearly framed as the hosts' own anecdote
segments.text:
Daniel: And finally, a small story from my own family, and it is entirely true.
Emma: That is how every invented story begins.
Daniel: My uncle kept a folded map of a town he never once visited.
Emma: Why?
Daniel: He liked knowing the way there. He folded it so often it came apart.
Emma: It came apart along the roads. That is almost poetry, Daniel.
Daniel: It came apart along the creases, which is worse and somehow better.
Emma: Beautiful. Nobody say another word. Let it play.

segments.flavor: a measured public-service style reminder with one dry twist
segments.text:
Daniel: The desk has a reminder, and the desk wants it on the record.
Emma: The desk is unusually formal about this.
Daniel: Stand up. Roll the shoulders back once. Then sit down again, a little lower.
Emma: Lower?
Daniel: The chair has been winning all afternoon. The shoulders would like a rematch.
Emma: Mine have conceded. They sit exactly where the chair tells them to sit.
Daniel: This is the most exercise The Brief has ever recommended, and the last.
Emma: Let the music do the rest of it.

segments.flavor: a calm time check and a one-line tease of what the rest of the hour holds
segments.text:
Daniel: It is nine minutes past the hour, and I will say that again shortly.
Emma: Why shortly?
Daniel: Because the time changes. It is the only part of the hour that does.
Emma: That is the most public radio sentence ever spoken inside this building.
Daniel: Ahead in this hour: one forecast, one correction, and one advertisement we stand behind.
Emma: We stand near it. Behind is a strong word, Daniel.
Daniel: We stand within clear sight of it. After that, a great deal of piano.
Emma: A great deal. Bring a chair and something warm to drink.
Daniel: Nine minutes past, and now ten. Told you. Here is the piano.

segments.flavor: back-announce the music stream in one warm sentence, then a dry observation from Emma
segments.text:
Daniel: That was thirty minutes of music without a single raised voice anywhere in it.
Emma: Thirty minutes, no shouting. Try that in any other room.
Daniel: Sky listened to the entire set outside, on a bench, wearing headphones.
Sky: [breathless] I did. I also ran for the bus during the slow part.
Emma: You ran during the slow part. That is the wrong part to run in.
Sky: The bus does not slow down for a double bass. I have asked.
Daniel: The double bass is unmoved by public transport. That is its entire character.
Emma: Unmoved, unhurried, unbothered. I would like to be a double bass.
Daniel: Then stand very still, and let this next one hold you up.

segments.flavor: a short 'and finally' style light story, invented but plausible, clearly framed as the hosts' own anecdote
segments.text:
Emma: And finally, from my own life, a story about a swimming pool.
Daniel: The desk is ready.
Emma: There was a lifeguard at that pool who blew his whistle at nobody.
Daniel: At nobody at all?
Emma: Empty water. Every twenty minutes. One short blast, then silence, then nothing.
Daniel: Perhaps he was simply keeping the water honest.
Emma: That is what I decided. The water behaved beautifully for the entire summer.
Daniel: Somewhere a pool is still being warned about something, and it has not moved.
Emma: I think about that whistle more often than I think about most people.
Daniel: Say nothing more about the lifeguard. The music can take it from here.

segments.flavor: a measured public-service style reminder with one dry twist
segments.text:
Daniel: A public service reminder, delivered slowly, because the fast ones never work.
Emma: Slow it down further. I have the whole hour.
Daniel: Check the spare tyre. Not now. But before the day you actually need it.
Emma: Nobody in history has checked a spare tyre on a calm afternoon.
Daniel: That is precisely when it should be checked. Calm is the correct weather.
Emma: Calm is the correct weather for everything, including this entire conversation.
Daniel: A spare tyre is a promise your past self made to your future self.
Emma: My past self promised a great deal. She was optimistic and had more time.
Daniel: Make one small promise this hour. Then let the saxophone take the rest.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: a kettle that refuses to hurry
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief is supported by Ambler Kettles, makers of the kettle that takes its time.
Emma: It takes four minutes. It will not be hurried and it does not explain itself.
Daniel: Ambler cannot promise the tea is better, only that you waited for it.
Emma: Ambler Kettles. Boil slowly. Now, back to the music.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: a desk lamp with one brightness
segments.text:
Daniel: Support for The Brief comes from Hollowell Desk Lamps, which have exactly one brightness.
Emma: One. There is no dial. There is no second setting. There is one.
Daniel: Hollowell believe a lamp should decide, so that you no longer have to.
Emma: Hollowell also believe a lamp cannot be argued with, and it cannot hear you.
Daniel: Hollowell Desk Lamps. One brightness, honestly. The music returns.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: an unlined notebook
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief is brought to you in part by Fennimore Notebooks, the unlined ones.
Emma: No lines. No grid. No dots. Nothing at all to disappoint you.
Daniel: A Fennimore page asks nothing of your handwriting, because it holds no opinion of it.
Emma: My handwriting needs an opinion. My handwriting needs close supervision.
Daniel: Fennimore. For thoughts that do not sit in tidy rows.
Emma: Fennimore accepts no responsibility for thoughts that sit in rows anyway. Music, please.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: an alarm clock that takes nine minutes
segments.text:
Daniel: Marlow Clocks support The Brief. A Marlow wakes you across nine full minutes.
Emma: Nine minutes of light, arriving the way a morning should, instead of all at once.
Daniel: No sound. No buzzing. Only a room slowly agreeing to be awake.
Emma: Marlow takes no responsibility for anyone who sleeps straight through a sunrise. Back to the jazz.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: a canvas bag built to outlast the trend
segments.text:
Daniel: Our sponsor is Pell and Daughter, who make one bag and have for decades.
Emma: It is canvas. It is beige. It holds far more than it should.
Daniel: Every seam is stitched twice, because the first stitch is only an opinion.
Emma: Pell and Daughter make no claim whatsoever about what you carry inside it.
Daniel: Pell and Daughter. A bag that outlives the trend. Music, gently.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: a radio that reports the weather already over
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief is supported by the Varden Weather Radio, a small grey box.
Emma: It reports the weather that has already happened, with total and quiet confidence.
Daniel: Sky has carried one in the field for a considerable stretch of time.
Sky: [breathless] It told me it had rained. I was already wet. It was correct.
Sky: It has never once been wrong. It has also never once been early.
Emma: Correct, and late. Varden call that being certain.
Daniel: The Varden Weather Radio. The weather you already survived, confirmed at last.
Emma: Varden accepts no liability for umbrellas bought too late. Here is the music.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: a plain archive box
segments.text:
Daniel: Support for The Brief comes from Cobb and Hale, who make the plain archive box.
Emma: Grey. Rectangular. Deeply uninterested in your feelings about paperwork.
Daniel: Each box holds one year of anything, and one blank label on the end.
Emma: The label is the hard part. Everyone stands there staring at the label.
Daniel: Cobb and Hale suggest writing the boring truth, and writing it in pen.
Emma: Miscellaneous is not a year. Miscellaneous is a decision you are avoiding.
Daniel: Cobb and Hale. Put it in the box. Close the lid.
Emma: Cobb and Hale cannot help with the box you labelled miscellaneous. Back to the horns.

segments.flavor: a sponsor only The Brief would have: coffee for the second half of the day
segments.text:
Daniel: The Brief is supported by Second Half, a coffee for the afternoon, decaffeinated.
Emma: It is coffee shaped. It is coffee coloured. It is not, technically, coffee.
Daniel: Second Half exists for the cup you want at four, not the one you need.
Emma: The ritual survives. The sleep survives. Everybody wins except the plant.
Daniel: Roasted slowly, in small batches, by people who do not rush anything at all.
Emma: Second Half makes no promise about the mug you left in the other room.
Daniel: Second Half. Drink the ritual, not the caffeine. Music now.

segments.flavor: the long pause, the only part of the hour with no words in it
segments.text:
Daniel: It is time now for the long pause, the only part of The Brief that carries no words.
Daniel: Four whole seconds of nothing at all, held completely on purpose, and then the piano walks in behind it.

segments.flavor: the correction desk
segments.text:
Daniel: A note now from the correction desk. Earlier in this hour I twice called a clarinet an oboe.
Daniel: The clarinet has now been told, the oboe forgave me at once, and the music resumes from here.

segments.flavor: the word of the hour
segments.text:
Daniel: It is time for the word of the hour. The word is petrichor.
Emma: Here we go.
Daniel: Petrichor is the smell of rain arriving on ground that has been dry.
Emma: There is a word for that, and none at all for finding the other sock.
Daniel: The priorities were settled long ago, and nobody thought to consult us.
Emma: Petrichor. Use it once, casually, and then never explain it to anyone.
Daniel: The word of the hour. And now, the music of the hour.

segments.flavor: the forecast for a town that does not exist
segments.text:
Daniel: Now the forecast for Greyhaven, a small coastal town that does not exist.
Emma: It never has. We forecast it anyway, every single hour, without fail.
Daniel: Sky has the conditions.
Sky: [breathless] Mist until the middle of the morning, then a long grey brightness.
Sky: The harbour is calm. Two boats are out. One of them is apparently ours.
Emma: We do not own a boat.
Sky: Greyhaven does not know that.
Daniel: Winds light. Visibility honest. Nothing will happen there, which is the entire appeal.
Emma: A full forecast for a town with no weather station and no residents.
Daniel: Greyhaven, out. The music has the rest of the hour.

segments.flavor: found objects, the things left behind in the studio
segments.text:
Daniel: Time for found objects, the small things left behind in this studio.
Emma: This hour: one glove. Left handed, wool, and very slightly damp.
Daniel: It has been sitting on the shelf for three weeks, waiting to be claimed.
Emma: It has stopped waiting. It has settled. It lives there now.
Daniel: We have given it a name. That was almost certainly a mistake.
Emma: Naming a glove ends any chance of returning it to a human being.
Daniel: The glove stays. Found objects will return. The music returns much sooner.

segments.flavor: the obituary, which on this station is always for an object
segments.text:
Daniel: And now the obituary, which on this station is always for an object.
Emma: This hour we mark the quiet passing of the studio stapler.
Daniel: It served eleven years without a single complaint and without a single jam.
Emma: It jammed constantly. We are being kind to the dead.
Daniel: It is survived by a box of staples that now fits nothing at all.
Emma: And by one paperclip it never once spoke to.
Daniel: The stapler asked for no flowers and it asked for no speeches.
Emma: It received a speech. It would have hated the speech.
Daniel: In its memory, we will hold things together loosely.
Emma: Very loosely. Now, music, for the stapler.

segments.flavor: the second opinion, in which one sentence gets rewritten
segments.text:
Daniel: Time now for the second opinion, in which Emma improves one sentence of mine.
Emma: The sentence was this. Conditions remain broadly unchanged across the whole region.
Daniel: It is accurate.
Emma: It is furniture. Nothing remains broadly anything. Say that nothing changed.
Daniel: Nothing changed.
Emma: Better. Shorter. True. That is the second opinion, and it was free.
Daniel: The desk accepts the correction, and the music accepts us back.

segments.flavor: the index, three numbers that describe the hour and nothing else
segments.text:
Daniel: Now the index, three numbers that describe this hour and nothing beyond it.
Emma: Number one is four. That is the count of mugs on this desk.
Daniel: Number two is one. That is how many mugs anyone is drinking from.
Emma: Number three is nine. The minutes since I last mentioned the mugs.
Daniel: The index is not a survey. The index is a small act of honesty.
Emma: It is also the only attention those mugs will get all hour.
Daniel: That is the index. The numbers reset. The music continues.
